claims.claim: A new Muslim makes ghusl in the first day or two (stated as advice, no ruling given)
claims.evidence: IslamQA (search snippets), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/81949/when-is-ghusl-required-and-when-is-it-mustahabb and https://islamqa.info/en/answers/975/causes-that-make-ghusl-a-must: 'The Malikis and Hanbalis are of the view that if a disbeliever becomes Muslim, ghusl is required ... The Hanafis and Shafi'is are of the view that it is encouraged'; 'If a disbeliever becomes Muslim when he is in the state of janabah, then he has to do ghusl.'

claims.claim: The Prophet told converts to make ghusl (basis of the practice)
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search snippet), https://sunnah.com/abudawud:355: Qays ibn Asim came to the Prophet intending to embrace Islam and was commanded to take a bath with water and lote-tree leaves; also in Tirmidhi and Nasa'i.

claims.claim: Ghusl on conversion is recommended, obligatory if in a state of major ritual impurity before praying
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (search snippet), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/islamic-belief/is-ghusl-required-after-saying-the-shahada-shaykh-abdul-rahim-reasat/: 'it is recommended that they perform a ritual bath'; 'only obligatory for the one who just enters Islam if they are in a state of major ritual impurity and are going to perform the prayers'.

rows.notes: Ghusl advice is consistent with the sources. The schools differ: Maliki and Hanbali say obligatory on conversion, Hanafi and Shafi'i say recommended unless the person was in a state of major impurity, in which case all agree it is needed before prayer. The description does not need to choose, but it could say 'before your first prayer'.
rows.method: 3 web searches (islamqa.info, sunnah.com, seekersguidance.org snippets); page fetch blocked

claims.claim: Hajj becomes an obligation once a person is able to go
claims.evidence: Quran.com, https://quran.com/ali-imran/97 (3:97): 'Pilgrimage to this House is an obligation by Allah upon whoever is able among the people'; the tafsir snippet on the same page explains 'able' as having sufficient provision and a means of transport, with a secure route.

claims.claim: Zakat becomes an obligation once its conditions (the nisab threshold) apply
claims.evidence: IslamQA, https://islamqa.info/en/answers/99381: if wealth falls short of the nisab, no zakah is due, and if it drops below the nisab during the year no zakah is due; https://islamqa.info/en/64: the nisab is 85 g of gold or 595 g of silver, the rate 2.5%, after one full lunar year.

rows.notes: Both statements are the standard Sunni position. Zakat also needs a full lunar year (hawl) on the wealth, which 'once the conditions apply' covers. Sending the reader to someone qualified is the right framing.

claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): Quran 2:187, eat and drink until the white thread of dawn is distinct from the black thread, then complete the fast until night; https://quran.com/2/187

claims.claim: 'In the Hanafi school' kissing or touching that leads to ejaculation breaks the fast
claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): all four Sunni schools hold that deliberate ejaculation from kissing or touching breaks the fast; they differ only on whether expiation is also due (Maliki: yes). The Hanafi label comes from the step's SeekersGuidance Hanafi source and implies the other schools allow it, which they do not.

claims.claim: The Prophet recommended breaking the fast with dates and water
claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): Sunan Abi Dawud 2356 (Anas): fresh dates, else dried dates, else sips of water; Sunan Abi Dawud 2355 and Tirmidhi 658 (Salman ibn Amir): break with dates, if not, water, for it is pure; https://sunnah.com/abudawud:2356. The step gives no hadith id for this.

claims.claim: Each day's fast needs a fresh intention (niyyah)
claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): this is the Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali position; the Maliki school holds that one intention at the start of Ramadan covers the whole month if the fast is not interrupted. Stated as agreed.

rows.notes: Two scope problems: 'in the Hanafi school' marks a point all four schools agree on, so a non-Hanafi reader may think it does not break their fast; the daily-intention rule is stated as agreed although the Maliki school accepts one intention for the month. Add a hadith id for dates and water (Abu Dawud 2356). Suhoor line is fine (Bukhari 1923).
rows.method: Compared with standard fiqh references and the step's cited SeekersGuidance (Hanafi) source note; not confirmed online (search budget exhausted, fetch blocked).

claims.claim: Pregnant or breastfeeding women may be exempt if fasting puts them at risk
claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): Sunan Abi Dawud 2408 and Tirmidhi 715 (Anas ibn Malik al-Ka'bi): Allah relieved the traveller of fasting and half the prayer, and the pregnant and nursing woman of fasting. claims.claim: Women do not fast during menstruation and make the days up
claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): Sahih Muslim 335 and Bukhari 321 (Aisha, asked by Mu'adhah): we were ordered to make up the fasts but not the prayers; https://sunnah.com/muslim:335

claims.claim: Older people who cannot fast feed a person in need per day; children are not required to fast

rows.notes: All six points are the standard Sunni positions. Precision point only: for pregnant and nursing women the schools differ on whether make-up days, fidyah or both follow, which the step rightly leaves to a scholar. Not confirmed online this session.

claims.claim: Ramadan follows the lunar calendar, so the dates shift each year
claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): the Islamic year is 354 or 355 days, so Ramadan begins about 10 to 11 days earlier each Gregorian year.

claims.claim: The month starts with the sighting of the new moon

In Canada some communities follow a calculated calendar (Fiqh Council of North America) and others a regional sighting committee, so local start dates can differ.

claims.claim: Tarawih nightly prayers, community iftars and Eid al-Fitr at the end of the month
claims.evidence: from standard references (not confirmed online): standard practice; Sahih al-Bukhari 2009 on night prayer in Ramadan; Eid al-Fitr falls on 1 Shawwal.

rows.notes: Accurate at the level written. Worth one line that Canadian masjids may announce different start dates because some use calculation and some local sighting. Not confirmed online this session.

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 297: the Prophet leaned on Aisha's lap and recited Quran while she was menstruating
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search snippet), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:297: the Prophet 'used to lean on my lap and recite Qur'an while I was in menses' (chapter on reciting in the lap of one's menstruating wife).

claims.claim: Sahih Muslim 298a: 'Your menstruation is not in your hand' (fetching the mat from the mosque)
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (search snippet), https://sunnah.com/muslim:298a: 'Get me the mat from the mosque. She said: I am menstruating. Upon this he remarked: Your menstruation is not in your hand.'

rows.notes: All three citations match Sunnah.com's wording and numbering. The quoted phrases are exact, and 'fetching something from the masjid' fairly describes the mat in the hadith.
rows.method: 3 WebSearch queries restricted to sunnah.com; page fetch blocked

claims.claim: Sahih Muslim 335c and Sahih al-Bukhari 321: missed fasts are made up, missed prayers are not; Bukhari 305: every Hajj rite except tawaf
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (snippets), https://sunnah.com/muslim:335c: 'we were ordered to complete the fasts, but were not ordered to complete the prayers'; https://sunnah.com/bukhari:321: 'he never ordered us to offer them (the prayers missed during menses)'; https://sunnah.com/bukhari:305: 'perform all the ceremonies of Hajj like the others, but do not perform the Tawaf'.

claims.claim: Sahih Muslim 302: 'Do everything except intercourse', and the Prophet's displeasure at cutting women off during their periods
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (snippet), https://sunnah.com/muslim:302: the Jews would not eat with or live with a menstruating woman; the Prophet said 'Do everything except intercourse'; his face changed when two companions asked whether to do as the Jews did.

claims.claim: Sunan Abi Dawud 212 ('what is above the waist-wrapper is lawful') and Sahih al-Bukhari 302 (izar during menses) as the basis of the barrier view
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (snippets), https://sunnah.com/abudawud:212: 'What is above the waist-wrapper is lawful for you'; https://sunnah.com/bukhari:302: 'he used to order her to put on an Izar' before fondling during her period.

claims.claim: Hanafi, Maliki and Shafi'i schools ask for a barrier between navel and knee; the Hanbali school allows everything except intercourse
claims.evidence: IslamQA (search snippet), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/36722: 'Imam Abu Hanifah, Imam Malik and al-Shafi'i were of the view that intimacy between the navel and the knee is haram, and Imam Ahmad was of the view that this is permissible'. SeekersGuidance (Hanafi, Yusuf Weltch), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/halal-and-haram/what-type-of-intimacy-is-permitted-between-a-husband-and-a-wife-during-her-menstruation/: 'Any contact between the navel and the knees must be done over a barrier... skin-to-skin contact anywhere else on her body is permissible.'

rows.notes: All hadith citations and the four-school summary match the sources. The site's own sources.json note says its SeekersGuidance answer covers the Hanafi view only; IslamQA 36722 supplies the school-by-school attribution and could be added as a source. The prayer-owed timing point is kept general, which is fine.
rows.method: 7 WebSearch queries (sunnah.com, islamqa.info, seekersguidance.org); page fetch blocked

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 324: menstruating women come out for Eid and the gathering of believers but keep away from the musalla
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (snippet), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:324 (Umm Atiyya): 'the menstruating women should come out and participate in the good deeds as well as the religious gathering of the faithful believers but the menstruating women should keep away from the Musalla'.

claims.claim: Hanafi and Shafi'i scholars (SeekersGuidance answers) list dua, dhikr, salawat, listening to Quran, charity and learning as open during menses
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (snippet), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/what-are-acts-of-worship-a-menstruating-woman-can-engage-in/: dhikr ('recommended in the Hanafi school for women in their periods to sit making dhikr in the place they normally pray'), dua, Quranic verses said with the intention of supplication, and listening to the Quran 'while pondering its deep meanings'; a Shafi'i counterpart 'Can a Woman Do These Acts of Worship during Her Menses?' is listed on the same site.

rows.notes: Bukhari 324 matches and the list of acts that carry on matches the cited SeekersGuidance answers; these points are agreed across the schools.
rows.method: 2 WebSearch queries (sunnah.com, seekersguidance.org); page fetch blocked

claims.claim: Hanafi and Shafi'i schools: no Quran recitation during menses; listening, looking and Quranic phrases as dua or dhikr are allowed
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (Shafi'i, snippet), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity-shafii-fiqh/can-a-menstruating-woman-read-and-touch-the-quran/: reciting is 'permissible if it is with the intention of remembrance, and not with the intention of Quran recitation' (Khatib Shirbini); the Hanafi answer on acts of worship gives the same dua and dhikr exception.

claims.claim: Maliki school: recitation is allowed while the bleeding continues
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (snippet), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/a-menstruating-woman-reciting-the-quran-the-maliki-position-sticking-to-one-school-and-the-path-of-taqwa/: 'the Maliki School permits reciting the Quran for the menstruating woman while her bleeding is continuous, unconditionally', and permits touching the mushaf for those learning or teaching.

claims.claim: IslamQA and an AMJA scholar allow reciting from memory; the AMJA answer allows touching the mushaf when needed and says a phone or tablet app is not a mushaf
claims.evidence: IslamQA (snippet), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/2564: 'permissible for a menstruating woman to recite the Quran from memory, not from the Mus-haf'. AMJA fatwa 86681 (snippet), https://www.amjaonline.org/fatwa/en/86681/question-about-reading-divine-text-while-in-menstruation: reciting during menstruation 'is counted and accepted'; 'Some scholars allowed touching the mushaf for menstruating women if there is a need'; 'an electronic device with the Qur'an on it, will not take the same ruling as a mushaf'.

claims.claim: Touching a printed mushaf: most scholars say not to; some allow it with a covering; the Hanafi school is careful about printed translations and tafsir
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance Shafi'i answer (snippet): 'The majority of scholars among the Companions, Followers, and the Imams of the four schools have agreed on the prohibition of a menstruating woman touching the Mushaf'; IslamQA 2564: 'forbidden to touch the mus-haf'. The covered-hand allowance and the Hanafi caution on translations were not shown in the snippets (standard references, not confirmed online).

rows.notes: The positions are stated accurately and attributed correctly; the section rightly declines to choose. Two lesser points were not visible in the snippets: the allowance to touch the mushaf through a covering (a Hanafi and Hanbali view) and the Hanafi caution about printed translations and tafsir.
rows.method: 5 WebSearch queries (seekersguidance.org x2, islamqa.info, amjaonline.org); page fetch blocked

claims.claim: Most schools say not to stay in the prayer hall during menses and differ on passing through
claims.evidence: IslamQA (snippets), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/33649 and https://islamqa.info/en/answers/60213: 'The majority of jurists of the four Schools of Fiqh are of the view that it is not permissible for a menstruating woman to enter and stay in the mosque'; 'simply passing through is allowed, if she needs to and she is certain that she will not make the mosque impure'. The Hanafi answer below bars entry altogether, so the schools do differ on passing through.

claims.claim: Classrooms, halls and offices may not count as the masjid; ask which rooms count (Hanafi answer on a hifz class)
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (snippet), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/can-a-menstruating-woman-enter-the-masjid-for-a-hifz-class/: in the Hanafi school a menstruating woman does not enter the masjid, 'and this applies to any area directly above and below what has been designated as a masjid', but 'if there is a part of the building which was excluded from being classed as a mosque... then she can enter that area'; it suggests holding the class in a separate classroom.

rows.notes: Both statements match the cited Hanafi answer and IslamQA's four-school summary. The advice to ask which rooms count as the masjid follows the Hanafi answer closely.
rows.method: 2 WebSearch queries (seekersguidance.org, islamqa.info); page fetch blocked

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 306: the Prophet told Fatima bint Abi Hubaish to leave prayer during her period, then wash and pray
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (snippet), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:306: 'I do not become clean (from bleeding). Shall I give up my prayers? ... No, because it is from a blood vessel and not the menses'; the hadith continues with leaving prayer for the period, then washing and praying.

claims.claim: A period ends with white discharge or complete dryness; the schools differ on these signs and on brown or yellow discharge
claims.evidence: IslamQA (snippet), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/317771: 'There are two signs of the end of the period: dryness and the white discharge'; most jurists accept dryness 'except for what was narrated from Imam Malik'; brownish or yellowish discharge after the end of menses 'is not menses' (Umm Atiyyah). SeekersGuidance (snippet), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity/what-is-the-difference-between-menstruation-and-istihada/: check with 'a piece of white cotton or tissue' and keep a record.

rows.notes: Bukhari 306 matches, and the end-of-period signs match IslamQA and the cited SeekersGuidance answer, including the note that the schools differ. 'Full-body wash' follows the site's ghusl wording rule.
rows.method: 3 WebSearch queries (sunnah.com, islamqa.info, seekersguidance.org); page fetch blocked

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 306: istihadah does not stop prayer; leave prayer only during the real period, then wash and pray
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (snippet), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:306: 'No, because it is from a blood vessel and not the menses' (Fatima bint Abi Hubaish).

claims.claim: Hanafi excused person: bleeding so constant that there is no time for wudu and a short obligatory prayer; one wudu per prayer time, lasting until the time ends
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (snippet), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity/what-is-the-ruling-regarding-excused-person/ and related answers: one is excused 'only if the issue... lasts for an entire prayer time, such that there is not enough of a gap of time to perform a valid wudu and prayer'; the wudu 'is vitiated by the exiting of the prayer time'.

claims.claim: Other schools use different day limits to sort a period from other bleeding
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (snippet), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/purity/what-is-the-difference-between-menstruation-and-istihada/: in the Shafi'i school blood 'beyond 15 days after your last period ended' is menstruation, less than 15 days is istihada; the Hanafi maximum period is 10 days (standard references).

rows.notes: All three points match the cited SeekersGuidance answers and Sunnah.com. The excused-person summary is a fair simplification of the Hanafi rule, and the text rightly sends readers to a doctor and a teacher.

claims.claim: Nifas follows the rules of a period: no prayer or fasting, make up the fasts but not the prayers; ghusl and pray when it stops
claims.evidence: IslamQA (snippet), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/319: 'If the woman sees that she is pure, which is when the bleeding stops, then she should do ghusl and start praying'; the make-up rule rests on Sahih Muslim 335c and Bukhari 321 (confirmed under R0477) and nifas is treated like hayd in all schools (standard references).

claims.claim: The schools set the longest length of nifas differently
claims.evidence: IslamQA (snippet), https://islamqa.info/en/answers/319: forty days is 'the view of Abu Haneefah and Ahmad'; 'Maalik, al-Shaafa'i and Ahmad, according to one report, said that the longest it may last is 60 days'; 'Most of the scholars have not set any limit for the minimum'. The topic's cited Sunan Abi Dawud 311 (Umm Salamah: 'would refrain (from prayer) for forty days or forty nights') was confirmed in a GitHub mirror of sunnah.com data, and Sunnah.com surfaced the parallel https://sunnah.com/abudawud:312.

rows.notes: The statements match IslamQA's summary of the schools and are phrased carefully. Lesser point: the grade the site's source note gives Abu Dawud 311 (Hasan Sahih, al-Albani) was not visible in the snippets. Medical advice is kept separate from the religious guidance.

claims.claim: Men do not wear gold or silk
claims.evidence: Sunan an-Nasa'i 5148 confirmed in a GitHub mirror of sunnah.com data (fawazahmed0/wiki-test): 'Gold and silk have been permitted for the females of my Ummah, and forbidden to the males', graded Sahih (Al-Albani); site-cited URL https://sunnah.com/nasai:5148 not reached directly.

claims.claim: Women cover everything except the face and hands before non-mahram men; Quran 24:31 head coverings over the chest, 33:59 outer garments; both sexes lower the gaze (24:30-31)
claims.evidence: Quran.com (snippets), https://quran.com/an-nur/31: 'tell the believing women to lower their gaze... Let them draw their veils over their chests'; https://quran.com/al-ahzab/59: 'draw their cloaks over their bodies... recognized as virtuous and not be harassed'. SeekersGuidance (Hanafi), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/a-detailed-exposition-of-the-fiqh-of-covering-ones-nakedness-awra/: a free woman's awra is 'her full body... except for the face, hands, and feet', with covering the feet advised as caution.

claims.claim: The women's swimming answer asks for loose clothing that is not thin
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (snippet), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/modesty/is-swimming-permissible-for-women-in-islam/: 'obligatory to cover oneself with loose, modest, and non-transparent clothing', women-only settings, and a married woman seeks her husband's permission.

claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (snippets), https://sunnah.com/muslim:261a: 'Ten are the acts according to fitra: clipping the moustache, letting the beard grow, using the tooth-stick, snuffing water in the nose, cutting the nails, washing the finger joints, plucking the hair under the armpits, shaving the pubes and cleaning one's private parts with water' (the narrator forgot the tenth, perhaps rinsing the mouth); https://sunnah.com/muslim:258: 'clipping the moustache, cutting the nails, plucking hair under the armpits, shaving the pubes... not be neglected far more than forty nights'.

claims.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 5892: keep the beards and cut the moustaches short; Ibn Umar cut what went past his fist
claims.evidence: Sunnah.com (snippet), https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5892: 'Do the opposite of what the pagans do. Keep the beards and cut the moustaches short'; whenever Ibn Umar performed Hajj or Umra he held his beard and cut whatever remained outside his hold.

claims.claim: SeekersGuidance: Hanafi wajib at a fist and shaving prohibited, Maliki unlawful (al-Dasuqi); Shafi'i relied-upon view recommended, shaving disliked not forbidden, majority hold shaving unlawful, all agree it is blameworthy
claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (snippets), https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/what-is-a-beard-in-the-hanafi-school/: 'In the Hanafi school, it is wajib for the beard to be a fistful'; 'according to Dasuqi... It is unlawful (haram) for a man to shave off his beard'; https://seekersguidance.org/answers/shafii-fiqh/ruling-shaving-shortening-beard-shafii-school/: al-Rafi'i and al-Nawawi 'ruled that to keep a full beard is merely recommended', shaving or shortening is 'disliked' and 'not sinful'. The 'majority' and 'blameworthy' lines were not shown in the snippet.

claims.claim: Ontario's creed policy (section 10.2) says dress and appearance rules must accommodate a religious beard short of undue hardship, with a bearded Sikh security guard as the example
claims.evidence: OHRC (snippet), https://www.ohrc.on.ca/en/policy-preventing-discrimination-based-creed/10-specific-cases: rules 'requiring no beards or head coverings... may come into direct conflict with religious requirements. When they do, there is a duty to accommodate the person, short of undue hardship'; a security company's policy 'requiring all security guards to wear a hat and be clean-shaven was found to have discriminated against a turbaned Sikh man'. The sub-section number 10.2 was not visible in the snippet.

rows.notes: The three hadith, both SeekersGuidance beard answers and the OHRC example all match. Minor: the Shafi'i answer's 'majority' and 'blameworthy' lines and the OHRC sub-section number were not visible in snippets, and the claim that the fitrah list applies to women apart from beard and moustache is standard but carries no citation.

claims.evidence: SeekersGuidance (Hanafi), 'What Are the Obligatory Acts of the Ritual Bath (Ghusl)?', https://seekersguidance.org/answers/hanafi-fiqh/what-are-the-obligatory-acts-of-the-ritual-bath-ghusl/ (snippet): 'The obligatory actions of the purificatory bath are: (1) To rinse out the mouth and (2) nose, and (3) to wash the entire body'.
